questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A shopkeeper sells three items at prices ₹1.5, ₹2.25 and ₹3.75 each. She wants to express the total bill amount for any combination using rational numbers.

(i) Are these prices rational numbers? Justify.
(ii) Express each price as a fraction in lowest terms.
(iii) If a customer buys 4 of the first, 6 of the second, and 2 of the third item, what is the total bill?
(iv) Is the total bill a rational number?
questions.answer:
(i) Yes — each can be written as a fraction of integers (1.5 = 3/2, 2.25 = 9/4, 3.75 = 15/4). All rationals.
(ii) 1.5 = 3/2; 2.25 = 9/4; 3.75 = 15/4.
(iii) Total = 4·(3/2) + 6·(9/4) + 2·(15/4) = 6 + 13.5 + 7.5 = ₹27.
(iv) Yes, 27 = 27/1 is rational. The sum and product of rationals are rational (closure).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A student wants to classify √2, √4, π, 22/7, 0.333... and -5/6 into rational and irrational numbers.

(i) Which of these are rational? Justify each.
(ii) Which are irrational? Justify each.
(iii) Is 22/7 = π?
(iv) Is every terminating decimal a rational number?
questions.answer:
(i) Rational: √4 = 2 (integer, hence rational); 22/7 (a fraction of integers); 0.333... = 1/3 (recurring decimal); -5/6 (fraction).
(ii) Irrational: √2 (cannot be written as p/q for integers p,q); π (non-terminating, non-recurring decimal).
(iii) No. 22/7 ≈ 3.142857... (recurring), while π ≈ 3.14159... (non-recurring). 22/7 is just a common rational approximation of π.
(iv) Yes — every terminating decimal can be written as p/q, e.g. 0.75 = 75/100 = 3/4.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The decimal expansion of 1/3 = 0.333..., 1/7 = 0.142857142857..., 5/8 = 0.625, and 22/7 = 3.142857142857... .

(i) Which of these are TERMINATING decimals?
(ii) Which are NON-TERMINATING RECURRING?
(iii) State the rule: a rational p/q in lowest terms has a terminating decimal iff q has only which prime factors?
(iv) Is 0.101001000100001... rational?
questions.answer:
(i) Terminating: 5/8 = 0.625.
(ii) Non-terminating recurring: 1/3, 1/7 and 22/7. The recurring pattern is what makes them rational.
(iii) p/q (in lowest terms) terminates iff q's prime factorisation contains only 2 and/or 5. Otherwise it recurs.
(iv) No — the gaps between 1s keep growing, so the decimal is non-terminating AND non-recurring. It's irrational.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Using Euclid's division algorithm, we can find the HCF of two positive integers a and b (a > b) by repeatedly applying a = bq + r, then replacing (a, b) with (b, r) until r = 0.

(i) Find the HCF of 56 and 90 using Euclid's algorithm.
(ii) State the fundamental theorem of arithmetic.
(iii) Express 90 as a product of primes.
(iv) If HCF(a, b) = 4 and LCM(a, b) = 60, find a × b.
questions.answer:
(i) 90 = 56·1 + 34; 56 = 34·1 + 22; 34 = 22·1 + 12; 22 = 12·1 + 10; 12 = 10·1 + 2; 10 = 2·5 + 0. HCF = 2.
(ii) Every composite number > 1 can be expressed as a product of primes, and this factorisation is unique except for the order of the factors.
(iii) 90 = 2 × 3² × 5.
(iv) a × b = HCF × LCM = 4 × 60 = 240.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Two numbers have HCF 12 and LCM 1080. One of the numbers is 60.

(i) State the relationship between HCF, LCM, and the product of two numbers.
(ii) Use it to find the other number.
(iii) Verify HCF(60, other) = 12.
(iv) Verify LCM(60, other) = 1080.
questions.answer:
(i) For any two positive integers a and b: a × b = HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b).
(ii) Other = (12 × 1080) / 60 = 12960 / 60 = 216.
(iii) 60 = 2² · 3 · 5; 216 = 2³ · 3³. HCF = 2² · 3 = 12 ✓.
(iv) LCM = 2³ · 3³ · 5 = 8 · 27 · 5 = 1080 ✓.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A mathematician claims: 'For any two rational numbers a and b with a < b, there exists a rational number c such that a < c < b. In fact, there are infinitely many such c.'

(i) Find one rational number between 1/3 and 1/2.
(ii) Find another rational number between 1/3 and 1/2 different from your answer in (i).
(iii) State, in your own words, why there are infinitely many rationals between any two rationals.
(iv) Does the same property hold for IRRATIONAL numbers between two rationals?
questions.answer:
(i) The mean: (1/3 + 1/2)/2 = (2/6 + 3/6)/2 = (5/6)/2 = 5/12. Check: 1/3 = 4/12 < 5/12 < 6/12 = 1/2 ✓.
(ii) Take 3/8: 1/3 ≈ 0.333, 3/8 = 0.375, 1/2 = 0.5 ✓.
(iii) Between any two rationals you can take their mean, which is again rational and strictly between them. Iterating gives infinitely many: a < (a+c)/2 < c < (c+b)/2 < b, and so on. Density of Q.
(iv) Yes — between any two rationals there are also infinitely many irrationals (e.g. between 1/3 and 1/2 lies (1/3 + (√2)/100) which is irrational).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A classmate insists '√2 + √3 must be rational because it's just a sum of square roots.'

(i) Compute √2 + √3 approximately (use √2 ≈ 1.414, √3 ≈ 1.732).
(ii) Suppose √2 + √3 = r where r is rational. Squaring both sides, derive a contradiction.
(iii) Conclude whether √2 + √3 is rational or irrational.
(iv) Give one more example of an irrational expression formed using square roots.
questions.answer:
(i) √2 + √3 ≈ 1.414 + 1.732 = 3.146 (approx).
(ii) If √2 + √3 = r, then squaring: 2 + 2√6 + 3 = r² ⇒ 2√6 = r² − 5 ⇒ √6 = (r² − 5)/2. The RHS is rational (since r is). So √6 would be rational — but √6 is irrational (6 isn't a perfect square). Contradiction.
(iii) √2 + √3 is IRRATIONAL.
(iv) Examples: √2 + √5, √7, 3 + √2, 1/√2 — all irrational.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A library maintains book IDs as integers from 1 to 1000. The librarian wants to group them by remainder mod 7.

(i) How many book IDs have remainder 0 when divided by 7?
(ii) How many have remainder 3?
(iii) Is the set of integers from 1 to 1000 partitioned by the seven remainder classes mod 7?
(iv) State the division algorithm for two positive integers in your own words.
questions.answer:
(i) Multiples of 7 in [1, 1000]: 7, 14, ..., 994. Number = ⌊1000/7⌋ = 142.
(ii) Numbers ≡ 3 (mod 7) in [1, 1000]: 3, 10, 17, ..., 997. Form 7k + 3 with k = 0..142. Count = 143.
(iii) Yes — every integer falls into EXACTLY ONE class (0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6 mod 7). Total: 142 + 143×6 = ... let's verify: total should be 1000. Counts are 142, 143, 143, 143, 143, 143, 143 ⇒ 142 + 6×143 = 142 + 858 = 1000 ✓.
(iv) For positive integers a and b (b > 0), there exist UNIQUE integers q (quotient) and r (remainder) with a = bq + r and 0 ≤ r < b.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The number 0.142857142857... has the recurring block '142857' of length 6.

(i) Convert 0.142857... (with bar over 142857) into a p/q form.
(ii) Why does the decimal expansion of 1/7 recur?
(iii) What is the maximum possible length of a recurring block for the fraction 1/n in terms of n?
(iv) Express 0.6̄ (i.e. 0.6666...) as a fraction.
questions.answer:
(i) Let x = 0.142857142857... Multiply by 10⁶: 10⁶·x = 142857.142857... Subtracting: 10⁶ x − x = 142857 ⇒ (10⁶ − 1) x = 142857 ⇒ x = 142857 / 999999 = 1/7.
(ii) Long division of 1 by 7 produces remainders cycling through {1,3,2,6,4,5} before returning to 1. Six distinct remainders forces a recurring block of length 6.
(iii) The block length for 1/n is at most n − 1 (since possible non-zero remainders are 1,2,...,n-1). When that maximum is reached, n is called a 'full reptend prime' (e.g. 7, 17, 19).
(iv) Let x = 0.6666... Then 10x = 6.6666...; subtracting: 9x = 6 ⇒ x = 6/9 = 2/3.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The prime factorisation of 360 is found using a factor tree.

(i) Find the prime factorisation of 360.
(ii) Hence find the prime factorisation of 360² = 129600.
(iii) How many positive divisors does 360 have?
(iv) If d is the number of divisors of a number whose prime factorisation is p₁^a · p₂^b · p₃^c, give a general formula for d.
questions.answer:
(i) 360 = 2³ · 3² · 5.
(ii) 360² = (2³ · 3² · 5)² = 2⁶ · 3⁴ · 5².
(iii) For 360 = 2³ · 3² · 5¹, number of divisors = (3+1)(2+1)(1+1) = 4·3·2 = 24.
(iv) For p₁^a · p₂^b · p₃^c, total divisors = (a+1)(b+1)(c+1). More generally, for p₁^a₁ · p₂^a₂ · ... · pₖ^aₖ: d = ∏(aᵢ + 1).
